{{short description|Concept in cosmology}}
{{redirect|Vacuum catastrophe}}
{{About|the problem relating to energy|the problem relating to galaxies|Hubble tension}}
{{Beyond the Standard Model}}

{{unsolved|physics|Why is the vacuum energy density much smaller than a zero-point energy suggested by quantum field theory?}}

In [[cosmology]], the '''cosmological constant problem''' or '''vacuum catastrophe''' is the substantial disagreement between the observed values of [[vacuum energy]] [[energy density|density]] (the small value of the [[cosmological constant]]) and the much larger theoretical value of [[zero-point energy]] suggested by [[quantum field theory]].

Depending on the [[Cutoff (physics)|cutoff]] of [[Planck energy]] and other factors, the quantum vacuum energy contribution to the effective cosmological constant is calculated to be between 50 and as many as 122 orders of magnitude greater than has actually been observed,<ref name="AdlerCasey1995"/><ref name="BengocheaLeónOkonSudarsky2020">{{cite journal |last1=Bengochea |first1=Gabriel R. |last2=León |first2=Gabriel |last3=Okon |first3=Elias |last4=Sudarsky |first4=Daniel |date=11 January 2020 |title=Can the quantum vacuum fluctuations really solve the cosmological constant problem? |journal=The European Physical Journal C |volume=80 |issue=18 |page=18 |doi=10.1140/epjc/s10052-019-7554-1  |doi-access=free|arxiv=1906.05406 |bibcode=2020EPJC...80...18B |s2cid=189762342 }}</ref> a state of affairs described by physicists as "the largest discrepancy between theory and experiment in all of science"<ref name="AdlerCasey1995"/> and "probably the worst theoretical prediction in the history of physics".<ref name=Hobson>{{cite book |author=MP Hobson, GP Efstathiou & AN Lasenby |year=2006 |title=General Relativity: An introduction for physicists  |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5dryXCWR7EIC&pg=PA187 |page=187 |edition=Reprint |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn=978-0-521-82951-9}}</ref>

==History==
The idea that empty space might contain zero-point radiation energy was proposed by [[Walther Nernst]] in 1916.<ref name=Nernst>
*{{cite journal
 |author=W Nernst
 |year=1916
 |title=Über einen Versuch von quantentheoretischen Betrachtungen zur Annahme stetiger Energieänderungen zurückzukehren
 |journal=Verhandlungen der Deutschen Physikalischen Gesellschaft
 |volume=18 |pages=83–116
 |doi=
 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=coo.31924056112240;view=1up;seq=93
|language=de}}
*{{cite web
 |author=W Nernst
 |date=January 1916
 |title=On an attempt to return from quantum theoretical considerations to the assumption of continuous energy changes; by W. Nernst.
 |url=https://www.roe.ac.uk/~jap/zpe/nernst1916.pdf
 |language=en
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260518213127/https://www.roe.ac.uk/~jap/zpe/nernst1916.pdf
 |archive-date=18 May 2026}}</ref><ref name=Kragh2011>
{{cite arXiv
 |author=H Kragh
 |year=2011
 |title= Preludes to dark energy: Zero-point energy and vacuum speculations
 |class=physics.hist-ph
 |eprint=1111.4623}}</ref><ref name=Kragh2012>
{{cite journal
 |author=H Kragh
 |year=2012
 |title= Walther Nernst: grandfather of dark energy?
 |journal= Astronomy & Geophysics
 |volume=53 |issue=1
 |pages=1.24–1.26
 |doi=10.1111/j.1468-4004.2012.53124.x
 |bibcode=2012A&G....53a..24K
 |language=en|doi-access=free
 }}</ref>
He predicted that the value had to be either zero or very small. In 1926, [[Wilhelm Lenz]] concluded that "If one allows waves of the shortest observed wavelengths {{math|''λ'' 	
≈ 2 × 10<sup>−11</sup>}} cm, ... and if this radiation, converted to material density ({{math|''u''/''c''<sup>2</sup> ≈ 10<sup>6</sup>}}), contributed to the curvature of the observable universe – one would obtain a vacuum energy density of such a value that the radius of the observable universe would not reach even to the Moon."<ref name=Lenz1926>
{{cite journal
 |author=W Lenz
 |year=1926
 |title= Das Gleichgewicht von Materie und Strahlung in Einsteins geschlossener Welt
 |journal= Physikalische Zeitschrift |volume=27 |pages=642–645
 |language=de}}</ref><ref name=Kragh2012/> [[Wolfgang Pauli]] reached the same conclusion in 1933.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=O’Raifeartaigh |first1=Cormac |last2=O’Keeffe |first2=Michael |last3=Nahm |first3=Werner |last4=Mitton |first4=Simon |date=2018-04-01 |title=One hundred years of the cosmological constant: from "superfluous stunt" to dark energy |url=https://doi.org/10.1140/epjh/e2017-80061-7 |journal=The European Physical Journal H |language=en |volume=43 |issue=1 |pages=73–117 |doi=10.1140/epjh/e2017-80061-7 |issn=2102-6467|arxiv=1711.06890 |bibcode=2018EPJH...43...73O }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Rham |first=Claudia de |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZU-GEQAAQBAJ&dq=energy+to+the+moon+pauli+lenz+vacuum&pg=PA134 |title=The Beauty of Falling: A Life in Pursuit of Gravity |date=2026-04-21 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-23750-3 |language=en}}</ref> The idea that the vacuum energy was related to the expansion of the universe was proposed by [[Georges Lemaître]] in 1934.<ref name=":1" />

After the development of quantum field theory in the 1940s and the observation of the expansion of the universe in the 1950s, the first to address contributions of quantum fluctuations to the cosmological constant was [[Yakov Zeldovich]] in the 1960s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zel'Dovich |first1=Ya. B. |title=Cosmological Constant and Elementary Particles |url=http://jetpletters.ru/ps/1673/article_25521.shtml |journal=JETP Letters |volume=6 |pages=316–317 |year=1967 |bibcode=1967JETPL...6..316Z }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zel'dovich |first1=Ya. B |title=The Cosmological Constant and the Theory of Elementary Particles |journal=Soviet Physics Uspekhi |date=31 March 1968 |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=381–393 |doi=10.1070/PU1968v011n03ABEH003927}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> In quantum mechanics, the vacuum itself should experience quantum fluctuations. In general relativity, those quantum fluctuations constitute energy that would add to the cosmological constant. However, Zeldovich calculated vacuum energy density was forty orders of magnitude bigger than the observed cosmological constant.<ref name=":1" /> 

In the 1970s, due to the discovery of the [[electroweak interaction]], another contribution was added to the cosmological constant due to [[spontaneous symmetry breaking]], increasing the discrepancy.<ref name=":1" /> Later estimates of the degree of mismatch were as high as 120 to 122 orders of magnitude;<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Weinberg |first=Steven |date=1989-01-01 |title=The cosmological constant problem |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/RevModPhys.61.1 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |language=en |volume=61 |issue=1 |pages=1–23 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.61.1 |bibcode=1989RvMP...61....1W |hdl=2152/61094 |s2cid=122259372 |issn=0034-6861|hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="afraid to ask" /> Modern research suggests that, when [[Lorentz transformation|Lorentz invariance]] is taken into account, the degree of mismatch is closer to 60 orders of magnitude.<ref name="afraid to ask" /><ref>{{Cite arXiv |last=Straumann |first=Norbert |date=2002 |title=The history of the cosmological constant problem |eprint=gr-qc/0208027 }}</ref>

With the development of [[inflationary cosmology]] in the 1980s, the problem became much more important: as cosmic inflation is driven by vacuum energy, differences in modeling vacuum energy lead to huge differences in the resulting cosmologies. Were the vacuum energy precisely zero, as was once believed, then the [[expansion of the universe]] would not [[Accelerating expansion of the universe|accelerate]] as observed, according to the standard [[Lambda-CDM model|Λ-CDM model]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Weinberg |first=Steven |date=1989-01-01 |title=The cosmological constant problem |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=61 |issue=1 |pages=1–23 |bibcode=1989RvMP...61....1W |doi=10.1103/revmodphys.61.1 |issn=0034-6861 |s2cid=122259372 |hdl-access=free |hdl=2152/61094}}</ref>

In 1989, [[Steven Weinberg]] showed that the different contributions to the cosmological constant cannot, under general conditions, cancel without fine tuning their values, this result became known as '''Weinberg's no-go theorem'''.'''<ref name=":1" />'''<ref name=":2" /> In the 2000s, Weinberg also proposed, what is sometimes called the '''new cosmological problem''', which consist in finding a theory that matches its non-zero value. The new cosmological problem is often equated with the [[cosmic coincidence problem]] (the fact that energy density from [[dark matter]] and dark energy are of the same order of magnitude today).<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite arXiv |last=Weinberg |first=Steven |title=The Cosmological Constant Problems (Talk given at Dark Matter 2000, February, 2000) |date=2000 |language=en |eprint=astro-ph/0005265 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Elizalde |first1=E. |date=2001-09-06 |title=Matching the observational value of the cosmological constant |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0370269301009212 |journal=Physics Letters B |language=en-US |volume=516 |issue=1–2 |pages=143–150 |doi=10.1016/S0370-2693(01)00921-2 |issn=0370-2693|arxiv=hep-th/0007094 }}</ref>

==Estimated values==
The vacuum energy density of the Universe based on 2015 measurements by the [[Planck (spacecraft)#Results|Planck collaboration]] is {{math|''ρ''{{sub|vac}}}} = {{val|5.96|e=-27|u=kg/m3}} ≘ {{val|5.3566|e=-10|u=J/m3}} = {{val|3.35|u=GeV/m3}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Planck Collaboration |last2=Ade |first2=P. A. R. |last3=Aghanim |first3=N. |last4=Arnaud |first4=M. |last5=Ashdown |first5=M. |last6=Aumont |first6=J. |last7=Baccigalupi |first7=C. |last8=Banday |first8=A. J. |last9=Barreiro |first9=R. B. |last10=Bartlett |first10=J. G. |last11=Bartolo |first11=N. |last12=Battaner |first12=E. |last13=Battye |first13=R. |last14=Benabed |first14=K. |last15=Benoît |first15=A. |date=2016 |title=Planck 2015 results: XIII. Cosmological parameters |url=http://www.aanda.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201525830 |journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics |volume=594 |pages=A13 |arxiv=1502.01589 |bibcode=2016A&A...594A..13P |doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201525830  |doi-access=free|issn=0004-6361}}</ref><ref group="note">Calculated based on the Hubble constant and the [[dark energy]] density parameter {{math|Ω{{sub|Λ}}}}.</ref> or about {{val|2.5|e=-47|u=GeV<sup>4</sup>}} in [[Geometrized unit system|geometrized unit]]s.

One assessment, made by Jérôme Martin of the [[Institut d'Astrophysique de Paris]] in 2012, placed the expected theoretical vacuum energy scale around 10<sup>8</sup> GeV<sup>4</sup>, for a difference of about 55 orders of magnitude.<ref name="afraid to ask" />

=== Cutoff dependence and renormalization ===
The calculated vacuum energy is a positive, rather than negative, contribution to the cosmological constant because the existing vacuum has negative quantum-mechanical ''pressure'', while in [[general relativity]], the gravitational effect of negative pressure is a kind of repulsion. (Pressure here is defined as the flux of [[Momentum#Quantum mechanical|quantum-mechanical momentum]] across a surface.) Roughly, the vacuum energy is calculated by summing over all known quantum-mechanical fields, taking into account interactions and self-interactions between the ground states, and then removing all interactions below a minimum "cutoff" wavelength to reflect that existing theories break down and may fail to be applicable around the cutoff scale. Because the energy is dependent on how fields interact within the current vacuum state, the vacuum energy contribution would have been different in the early universe; for example, the vacuum energy would have been significantly different prior to [[Spontaneous symmetry breaking#Higgs mechanism|electroweak symmetry breaking]] during the [[Chronology of the universe#Electroweak symmetry breaking|quark epoch]].<ref name="afraid to ask">{{cite journal |last1=Martin |first1=Jérôme |date=July 2012 |title=Everything you always wanted to know about the cosmological constant problem (but were afraid to ask) |journal=Comptes Rendus Physique |volume=13 |issue=6–7 |pages=566–665 |arxiv=1205.3365 |bibcode=2012CRPhy..13..566M |doi=10.1016/j.crhy.2012.04.008 |s2cid=119272967}}</ref>

The vacuum energy in quantum field theory can be set to any value by [[renormalization]]. This view treats the cosmological constant as simply another fundamental physical constant not predicted or explained by theory.<ref>{{cite journal
 |year=2002 
 |title=The quantum vacuum and the cosmological constant problem
 |url=http://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/398/
 |journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics
 |volume=33 |pages=663–705
 |doi=10.1016/S1355-2198(02)00033-3
 |issue=4
 |bibcode = 2002SHPMP..33..663R |arxiv=hep-th/0012253|s2cid=9007190 
 |last1=Rugh
 |first1=S.E.
 |last2=Zinkernagel
 |first2=H.
 }}</ref> Such a renormalization constant must be chosen very accurately because of the many-orders-of-magnitude discrepancy between theory and observation, and many theorists consider this ad-hoc constant as equivalent to ignoring the problem.<ref name="AdlerCasey1995">{{cite journal|last1=Adler|first1=Ronald J.|last2=Casey|first2=Brendan|last3=Jacob|first3=Ovid C.|title=Vacuum catastrophe: An elementary exposition of the cosmological constant problem|journal=American Journal of Physics|volume=63|issue=7|year=1995|pages=620–626|issn=0002-9505|doi=10.1119/1.17850|bibcode=1995AmJPh..63..620A|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Using [[Planck units|Planck mass]] as the cut-off for a cut-off regularization scheme provides a difference of 120 orders of magnitude between the vacuum energy and the cosmological constant.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last1=Calcagni |first1=Gianluca |title=Lectures on classical and quantum cosmology |date=2022-11-23 |work=Proceedings of Corfu Summer Institute 2021 "School and Workshops on Elementary Particle Physics and Gravity" — PoS(CORFU2021) |volume=406 |page=317 |url=https://pos.sissa.it/406/317/ |access-date=2025-09-03 |publisher=SISSA Medialab |language=en |last2=Di Luca |first2=Maria Grazia |last3=Fodran |first3=Tomáš |doi=10.22323/1.406.0317 |doi-access=free |hdl=10261/350802 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> However this method violates [[Lorentz covariance]].<ref name=":0" /> Using [[dimensional regularization]] instead, reduces this difference to about 56 orders of magnitude.<ref name=":0" />

==Proposed solutions==
Some proposals involve modifying gravity to diverge from general relativity. These proposals face the hurdle that the results of observations and experiments so far have tended to be extremely consistent with general relativity and the ΛCDM model, and inconsistent with thus-far proposed modifications. In addition, some of the proposals are arguably incomplete, because they solve the "new" cosmological constant problem by proposing that the actual cosmological constant is exactly zero rather than a tiny number, but fail to solve the "old" cosmological constant problem of why quantum fluctuations seem to fail to produce substantial vacuum energy in the first place. Nevertheless, many physicists argue that, due in part to a lack of better alternatives, proposals to modify gravity should be considered "one of the most promising routes to tackling" the cosmological constant problem.<ref name="dark universe"/>

[[W. G. Unruh|Bill Unruh]] and collaborators have argued that when the energy density of the quantum vacuum is modeled more accurately as a fluctuating quantum field, the cosmological constant problem does not arise.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wang |first1=Qingdi |last2=Zhu |first2=Zhen |last3=Unruh |first3=William G. |author-link3=W. G. Unruh |title=How the huge energy of quantum vacuum gravitates to drive the slow accelerating expansion of the Universe |journal=[[Physical Review D]] |volume=95 |issue=10 |year=2017 |article-number=103504 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.95.103504 |arxiv=1703.00543|bibcode=2017PhRvD..95j3504W |s2cid=119076077 }}</ref> Going in a different direction, [[George F. R. Ellis]] and others have suggested that in [[unimodular gravity]], the troublesome contributions simply do not gravitate.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Ellis |first=George F. R. |author-link=George F. R. Ellis |title=The trace-free Einstein equations and inflation |journal=[[General Relativity and Gravitation]] |year=2014 |volume=46 |article-number=1619 |doi=10.1007/s10714-013-1619-5 |arxiv=1306.3021|bibcode=2014GReGr..46.1619E |s2cid=119000135 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Percacci |first=R. |title=Unimodular quantum gravity and the cosmological constant |doi=10.1007/s10701-018-0189-5 |arxiv=1712.09903 |year=2018 |journal=[[Foundations of Physics]] |volume=48 |number=10 |pages=1364–1379|bibcode=2018FoPh...48.1364P |s2cid=118934871 }}</ref> Recently, a fully diffeomorphism-invariant action principle that gives the equations of motion for trace-free Einstein gravity has been proposed, where the cosmological constant emerges as an integration constant.<ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=2312.03062|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.108.124013|title=Diffeomorphism-invariant action principles for trace-free Einstein gravity|year=2023|last1=Montesinos|first1=Merced|last2=Gonzalez|first2=Diego|journal=Phys. Rev. D|volume=108|issue=12|article-number=124013 |bibcode=2023PhRvD.108l4013M }}</ref>

Another argument, due to [[Stanley Brodsky]] and Robert Shrock, is that in [[light front quantization]], the [[quantum field theory]] vacuum becomes essentially trivial. In the absence of vacuum expectation values, there is no contribution from [[quantum electrodynamics]], [[weak interactions]], and [[quantum chromodynamics]] to the cosmological constant. It is thus predicted to be zero in a flat [[spacetime]].<ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=1005.4610|doi=10.1103/PhysRevC.82.022201|title=New perspectives on the quark condensate|year=2010|last1=Brodsky|first1=Stanley J.|last2=Roberts|first2=Craig D.|last3=Shrock|first3=Robert|last4=Tandy|first4=Peter C.|journal=Physical Review C|volume=82|issue=2|article-number=022201|bibcode=2010PhRvC..82b2201B}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=1202.2376|doi=10.1103/PhysRevC.85.065202|title=Confinement contains condensates|year=2012|last1=Brodsky|first1=Stanley J.|last2=Roberts|first2=Craig D.|last3=Shrock|first3=Robert|last4=Tandy|first4=Peter C.|journal=Physical Review C|volume=85|issue=6|article-number=065202|bibcode=2012PhRvC..85f5202B|s2cid=118373670}}</ref> From [[light front quantization]] insight, the origin of the cosmological constant problem is traced back to unphysical [[Causality_(physics)|non-causal]] terms in the standard calculation, which lead to an erroneously large value of the cosmological constant.<ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=2202.06051|doi=10.1038/s42254-022-00453-3|title=Artificial dynamical effects in quantum field theory|year=2022|last1=Brodsky|first1=Stanley J.|last2=Deur|first2=Alexandre|last3=Roberts|first3=Craig D.|journal=Nature Rev. Phys.|volume=4|issue=7|page=489 |bibcode=2022NatRP...4..489B }}</ref>

In 2018, a mechanism for cancelling Λ out has been proposed through the use of a [[symmetry breaking]] potential in a Lagrangian formalism in which matter shows a non-vanishing pressure. The model assumes that standard matter provides a pressure which counterbalances the action due to the cosmological constant. Luongo and Muccino have shown that this mechanism permits to take vacuum energy as [[quantum field theory]] predicts, but removing the huge magnitude through a counterbalance term due to [[baryons]] and [[cold dark matter]] only.<ref name="Luongo Muccino pp. 2-3">{{cite journal |last1=Luongo |first1=Orlando |last2=Muccino |first2=Marco |title=Speeding up the Universe using dust with pressure |journal=Physical Review D |volume=98 |issue=10 |date=2018-11-21 |issn=2470-0010 |doi=10.1103/physrevd.98.103520 |pages=2–3|arxiv=1807.00180 |bibcode=2018PhRvD..98j3520L |s2cid=119346601 }}</ref>

In 1999, [[Andrew Cohen (scientist)|Andrew Cohen]], [[David B. Kaplan]] and [[Ann Nelson]] proposed that correlations between the [[Cutoff (physics)|UV and IR cutoffs]] in [[effective field theory|effective]] [[quantum field theory]] are enough to reduce the theoretical cosmological constant down to the measured cosmological constant due to the Cohen–Kaplan–Nelson (CKN) bound.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Effective Field Theory, Black Holes, and the Cosmological Constant|last1=Cohen|first1=Andrew|last2=Kaplan|first2=David B.|last3=Nelson|first3=Ann|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=82|issue=25|date=21 June 1999|pages=4971–4974|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.82.4971|arxiv=hep-th/9803132|bibcode=1999PhRvL..82.4971C|s2cid=17203575}}</ref> In 2021, Nikita Blinov and Patrick Draper confirmed through the [[holographic principle]] that the CKN bound predicts the measured cosmological constant, all while maintaining the predictions of effective field theory in less extreme conditions.<ref>{{cite arXiv|title=Densities of States and the CKN Bound|author1=Nikita Blinov|author2=Patrick Draper|eprint=2107.03530|date=7 July 2021|class=hep-ph}}</ref>

Some propose an anthropic solution,<ref name="Totani2019">{{cite journal |last1=Totani |first1=Tomonori |last2=Omiya |first2=Hidetoshi |last3=Sudoh |first3=Takahiro |last4=Kobayashi |first4=Masakazu A. R. |last5=Nagashima |first5=Masahiro |date=2 January 2019 |title=Lethal Radiation from Nearby Supernovae Helps Explain the Small Cosmological Constant |url=https://www.liebertpub.com/doi/abs/10.1089/ast.2018.1895 |journal=Astrobiology |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=126–131 |doi=10.1089/ast.2018.1895 |pmid=30129784 |arxiv=1804.10395 |bibcode=2019AsBio..19..126T |s2cid=133086904 |access-date=21 October 2022}}</ref> and argue that we live in one region of a vast [[multiverse]] that has different regions with different vacuum energies. These [[anthropic argument]]s posit that only regions of small vacuum energy such as the one in which we live are reasonably capable of supporting intelligent life. Such arguments have existed in some form since at least 1981. Around 1987, [[Steven Weinberg]] estimated that the maximum allowable vacuum energy for gravitationally-bound structures to form is problematically large, even given the observational data available in 1987, and concluded the anthropic explanation appears to fail; however, more recent estimates by Weinberg and others, based on other considerations, find the bound to be closer to the actual observed level of dark energy.<ref name=linde/><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Martel|first1=Hugo|author2-link=Paul R. Shapiro|last2=Shapiro|first2=Paul R.|last3=Weinberg|first3=Steven|title=Likely Values of the Cosmological Constant|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|date=January 1998|volume=492|issue=1|pages=29–40|doi=10.1086/305016|arxiv=astro-ph/9701099|bibcode=1998ApJ...492...29M|s2cid=119064782}}</ref> Anthropic arguments gradually gained credibility among many physicists after the discovery of dark energy and the development of the theoretical [[string theory landscape]], but are still derided by a substantial skeptical portion of the scientific community as being problematic to verify. Proponents of anthropic solutions are themselves divided on multiple technical questions surrounding how to calculate the proportion of regions of the universe with various dark energy constants.<ref name=linde>{{cite journal |last1=Linde |first1=Andrei |title=A brief history of the multiverse |journal=Reports on Progress in Physics |date=1 February 2017 |volume=80 |issue=2 |page=022001 |doi=10.1088/1361-6633/aa50e4|pmid=28071600 |arxiv=1512.01203 |bibcode=2017RPPh...80b2001L |s2cid=5221573 }}</ref><ref name="dark universe">{{cite journal |last1=Bull |first1=Philip |display-authors=etal |title=Beyond ΛCDM: Problems, solutions, and the road ahead |journal=Physics of the Dark Universe |date=June 2016 |volume=12 |pages=56–99 |doi=10.1016/j.dark.2016.02.001|arxiv=1512.05356 |bibcode=2016PDU....12...56B |s2cid=118450389 }}</ref>
